VERDICT: PASS
REASON: After reviewing the repository’s production code paths that perform filesystem I/O, no evidence was found of a production-reachable attacker-controlled input (per the provided trust model) flowing into a filesystem sink in a way that can escape an intended base directory. The places where strings are used to construct on-disk paths (e.g., deploymentName, contextRoot, timer IDs, external mounts) are driven by server configuration/deployment metadata and management operations, i.e., admin/operator-controlled rather than remote/low-privilege attacker-controlled as documented in this repo.
EVIDENCE: 
- WildFly repo docs describe server startup/stop via local scripts and admin console/CLI (management by operators/admins), with no mention of unauthenticated/low-priv deployment/upload interfaces in this repo’s docs: [/README.md:1-41].
- Deployment-time path concatenation without canonical containment (but sourced from deployment unit names, not request input): temp directory for a deployment is created under the server TEMP_DIR using a computed deploymentName (deployment unit name / parent name): [/undertow/src/main/java/org/wildfly/extension/undertow/deployment/WarStructureDeploymentProcessor.java:137-151].
- Deployment-controlled “external mounts” feature reads a file inside the WAR (WEB-INF/external-mounts) and treats each non-comment line as a filesystem path (new File(trimmed)), but this is deployment-time and depends on deployment content rather than runtime request parameters: [/undertow/src/main/java/org/wildfly/extension/undertow/deployment/WarStructureDeploymentProcessor.java:160-184]. (Needs product clarification only if your production threat model treats deployment artifacts as attacker-controlled.)
- Webservices integration creates a document root directory under serverTempDir using jbwebMD.getContextRoot() (deployment metadata) with no shown canonicalization, but again this is internal/deployment-driven: [/webservices/server-integration/src/main/java/org/jboss/as/webservices/publish/EndpointPublisherImpl.java:197-209] and [/webservices/server-integration/src/main/java/org/jboss/as/webservices/util/WebAppController.java:88-99].
- Persistent session storage writes/reads a file under baseDir using deploymentName directly (no containment check), but deploymentName is a deployment identifier, not request input: [/undertow/src/main/java/org/wildfly/extension/undertow/DiskBasedModularPersistentSessionManager.java:69-128]. (Needs product clarification only if untrusted parties can choose deploymentName in production.)
- EJB timer persistence stores timer files under baseDir using timedObjectId with path-separator replacement (mitigates direct separator-based traversal in that component) and uses File I/O for timer persistence: [/ejb3/src/main/java/org/jboss/as/ejb3/timerservice/persistence/filestore/FileTimerPersistence.java:404-428].
- Example of a production HTTP-facing handler in this repo (ActiveMQ HTTP upgrade) processes request headers and network upgrade only; it does not perform filesystem I/O or construct filesystem paths from request data: [/messaging-activemq/src/main/java/org/wildfly/extension/messaging/activemq/HTTPUpgradeService.java:103-173].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The checked-in source code and resources in this repo do not provide direct evidence of an exploitable XSS (CWE-79): the only obvious browser-rendered pages included in-tree are static welcome-content HTML pages, and a scan of non-test sources did not find dynamic HTML generation or DOM-style sinks. However, WildFly’s real deployment includes a web-based management console that is pulled in and packaged from external Maven artifacts (not present in the repo tree), so I cannot verify whether those shipped console resources (HTML/JS) correctly neutralize attacker-controlled input.
EVIDENCE:
- Static welcome page shipped in-tree (no attacker-controlled templating): [/servlet-feature-pack/src/main/resources/content/welcome-content/index.html:22-55]
- /console redirect handler is part of the Undertow subsystem; it routes requests to the management console (or static “no console/no redirect” pages) and uses the request Host header to assemble redirect URIs, indicating a browser-facing surface exists even though no HTML rendering is done here: [/undertow/src/main/java/org/wildfly/extension/undertow/ConsoleRedirectService.java:47-170]
- The build declares a dependency on the HAL management console “release-stream” resources (classifier "resources"), which are expected to be packaged into the WildFly distribution but are not present in the repository for inspection: [/pom.xml:157-160] and [/pom.xml:4781-4824]

Needs product clarification / additional info required to reach PASS/FAIL:
- The actual contents of the shipped management console web assets assembled from the Maven dependency org.jboss.hal:release-stream:${version} with classifier resources, as packaged into the WildFly distribution (e.g., the resulting console .war/.jar/static resource tree), so its handling of untrusted input in HTML/DOM contexts can be evaluated.
- A precise list of other packaged web UIs (if any) in the distribution built from this repo (e.g., any additional console/admin UIs pulled from Maven dependencies), since those could also introduce CWE-79 issues even if not present as source here.

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Review of the WildFly Application Server codebase did not find any production-reachable use of attacker-influenced strings/ASTs/templates being evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (e.g., javax.script ScriptEngine, Groovy/MVEL/OGNL/SpEL/Janino, etc.). The primary expression-related code in this repo is limited to wiring/wrapping the JSP/JSF ExpressionFactory (expressions come from application templates/descriptors, not remote request data), and common template engines (Velocity/Mustache) appear only as private JBoss Modules (not used by server logic and not exposed as a WildFly “public API surface” meant to accept untrusted template text).
EVIDENCE:
- Repo is WildFly Application Server (i.e., a Java EE server runtime; production entry points are server subsystems, not a library that intentionally evaluates caller-provided code strings): [/workdir/repo/README.md:1-55].
- No hits for javax.script/ScriptEngine in non-test code; BeanShell appears only in documentation example; Velocity/Mustache appear as dependencies/modules but not as runtime evaluation callsites in this repo: [/evidence/artifacts/cwe94_sink_search.txt:1-22].
- JSP/EL integration in Undertow only wraps an ExpressionFactory obtained from Jasper and returns it; it does not parse/evaluate attacker-provided expression strings: [/workdir/repo/undertow/src/main/java/org/wildfly/extension/undertow/deployment/JspApplicationContextWrapper.java:39-80].
- ExpressionFactoryWrapper is an interface for wrapping the ExpressionFactory (no evaluation/compilation API provided here): [/workdir/repo/web-common/src/main/java/org/jboss/as/web/common/ExpressionFactoryWrapper.java:1-18].
- Velocity and Mustache are packaged as JBoss Modules marked `jboss.api` = `private`, supporting that they are not intended as exposed/public API surface of the WildFly artifact itself: [/workdir/repo/feature-pack/src/main/resources/modules/system/layers/base/org/apache/velocity/main/module.xml:25-33], [/workdir/repo/feature-pack/src/main/resources/modules/system/layers/base/com/github/spullara/mustache/main/module.xml:25-33].

There's a risk of template injection if an attacker controls the template text, but typically, developers create the templates, and untrusted data is only used as safe variables. metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repo is a Java library (XStream). The only notable “restricted parent directory” filesystem surface is the persistence package, which writes/reads per-key XML files under a caller-supplied base directory. The shipped implementations derive filenames by escaping path separators ("/" and "\\") and other absolute-path characters (e.g., ":"), so attacker-controlled key strings cannot influence the filesystem sink to resolve outside the base directory. No other production-relevant archive extraction or baseDir+untrusted-relative-path I/O surfaces were found.
EVIDENCE:
- Persistence strategy performs filesystem sinks using a base directory + derived filename (the containment boundary) via FileInputStream/FileOutputStream: writeFile(FileOutputStream) and put() uses `new File(baseDirectory, filename)`; get()/remove() read from `new File(baseDirectory, filename)` [/workdir/repo/xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/persistence/AbstractFilePersistenceStrategy.java:141-184,195-203].
- FilePersistenceStrategy (preferred, non-deprecated) escapes illegal filename characters including both path separators and colon by default (`"<>?:/\\\"|*%"` includes `/`, `\\`, `:`), and `getName` uses this escaping to produce the on-disk filename [/workdir/repo/xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/persistence/FilePersistenceStrategy.java:56-58,127-158].
- Deprecated FileStreamStrategy also prevents separators by allowing only alphanumeric characters in filenames and escaping everything else (including `/` and `\\`) into `_hex_` sequences [/workdir/repo/xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/persistence/FileStreamStrategy.java:84-103].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: This repository is XStream (a Java XML serialization/deserialization library) and ships an exposed API (XStream#fromXML) that is plausibly used on untrusted XML in downstream apps. The codebase contains no direct OS command/process execution calls, and it explicitly blocks automatic conversion of java.beans.EventHandler (a known deserialization-time gadget that can trigger ProcessBuilder.start()). However, XStream’s deserialization design still allows attacker-controlled XML to influence which classes are instantiated and it invokes serialization hooks (readResolve/readObject) on deserialized types. Whether this becomes an exploitable CWE-78 in a real deployment depends on (a) whether untrusted XML reaches fromXML in production and (b) what gadget classes (in the application’s classpath) are available/allowed such that deserialization-time execution can reach Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder.start with attacker-controlled arguments. The repo alone does not provide enough concrete evidence of a production-reachable OS-process-execution path.

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: This repository is the XStream Java object↔XML serialization library and does not implement a production web server/UI where attacker-controlled input is rendered into browser-executable contexts. The only HTML templating present is for generating the project’s static documentation site at build/package time, using local source content (not remote attacker-controlled input). Additionally, XStream’s default XML writer escapes the key metacharacters (<, >, &, quotes) in element text and attribute values, preventing markup/script injection through normal serialization output.
EVIDENCE: 
- Repo purpose is XML serialization (not a web app): root Maven description states “XStream is a serialization library from Java objects to XML and back.” [pom.xml:20-27]; core API javadoc describes XStream as a “Java-XML serialization tool” and shows `toXML()`/`fromXML()` usage [xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/XStream.java:144-155].
- Website HTML templating exists only for static site generation during build/package: xsite-maven-plugin uses `templates/skin.html` and runs in Maven `package` phase, writing to `${project.build.directory}/xsite` and copying into `${project.build.directory}/docs` [xstream-distribution/pom.xml:44-103].
- The shipped XML writer performs context-appropriate XML escaping for text and attributes (escaping &, <, >, ", ' and CR): documented behavior [xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/io/xml/PrettyPrintWriter.java:22-29] and implementation escaping these characters in `writeText`/`writeAttributeValue` [xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/io/xml/PrettyPrintWriter.java:217-305].
- The Freemarker skin template interpolates variables like `${title}`/`${body}` into HTML [xstream-distribution/src/templates/skin.html:14-55], but per the build configuration above it is used to generate static docs during packaging, not as a runtime web rendering surface exposed to remote/low-privilege users [xstream-distribution/pom.xml:44-103].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

REASON: The XStream library’s public deserialization API (fromXML/unmarshal) interprets attacker-supplied XML node names / class attributes as Java class names and loads them via Class.forName during unmarshalling. This is an exposed, shipped API surface that plausibly processes untrusted XML in downstream apps, enabling attacker-controlled class loading/instantiation (i.e., code selection/execution) without an allowlist or other effective restriction.
EVIDENCE:
- Public deserialization API surface: XStream’s Javadoc and fromXML methods show intended use to deserialize from an XML string/reader and call into unmarshal: [/xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/XStream.java:144-155] and [/xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/XStream.java:1003-1019].
- Unmarshal delegates into the unmarshalling pipeline (marshallingStrategy.unmarshal with mapper): [/xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/XStream.java:1161-1165].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repo’s production code (OSGi XSSAPI/XSSFilter services) performs HTML/JSON escaping and AntiSamy-based sanitization and does not invoke OS command/process execution APIs. The only command-related content is an ESAPI configuration allowlist entry, but there is no code in this repo that calls ESAPI’s Executor or any other process-execution sink.
EVIDENCE:
- The primary production service implementation XSSAPIImpl uses ESAPI’s Validator/Encoder and OWASP Java Encoder, plus XML parsing utilities; it contains no Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder usage or similar sinks. See imports and logic in [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/XSSAPIImpl.java:19-47] and example methods like getValidInteger/getValidHref that only validate/encode strings [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/XSSAPIImpl.java:80-219].
- The XSSFilter implementation loads AntiSamy policy files and uses AntiSamy to scan/filter input; it does not execute external processes. See policy loading and filtering flow in [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/XSSFilterImpl.java:107-201] and the isValidHref logic [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/XSSFilterImpl.java:243-251].
- PolicyHandler constructs AntiSamy/Policy objects from an InputStream and performs no OS execution [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/PolicyHandler.java:38-57].
- The only repository occurrence of an OS command string is in ESAPI.properties, configuring the ESAPI Executor allowlist (cmd.exe/runas.exe), but this repo’s code does not reference ESAPI Executor at all [/src/main/resources/ESAPI.properties:337-342].
- The bundle embeds ESAPI/AntiSamy/Encoder as dependencies, but the project’s own implementation package is marked private in the OSGi bundle configuration, indicating the library’s intended surface is the XSS services rather than command execution [/pom.xml:100-115].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repo ships an XSS-protection API (org.apache.sling.xss.XSSAPI) that explicitly claims to validate content for placement inside <script>...</script> or <style>...</style> blocks, but its implementation only forbids the JavaScript/CSS comment terminator "*/". It does not neutralize HTML parser break-out sequences such as "</script>", which would end the script block and allow attacker-supplied markup/script execution in a victim’s browser when the API is used as intended.
EVIDENCE:
- This is a shipped OSGi bundle/artifact providing XSS-protection services: packaging is a "bundle" and described as “XSS protection” based on AntiSamy/Encoder. [/pom.xml:33-40]
- The public API contract explicitly states the method is for use inside <script> or <style> blocks (a browser-executable output context): [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/XSSAPI.java:124-133]
- The implementation of that validator only checks for the substring "*/" and otherwise returns the attacker-controlled input unchanged, meaning sequences like "</script>" are not neutralized at all: [/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/XSSAPIImpl.java:307-316]
- Repo documentation positions the bundle as providing escaping/filtering for “XSS-prone user submitted content,” making untrusted-input usage plausible downstream: [/README.md:1-7]

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository is an Apache Sling OSGi bundle that provides XSS validation/encoding/sanitization services. In the production-relevant code paths and exposed API surface (XSSAPI/XSSFilter), inputs are validated/encoded or sanitized via AntiSamy scanning; there is no evidence of attacker-influenced strings being evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code, nor of embedded expression/template engines or scripting runtimes. The build configuration also explicitly excludes BeanShell (bsh), a common code-evaluation component.
EVIDENCE: 
- The shipped/public APIs are validators/encoders/filters and do not expose any “evaluate/compile/execute expression/template” capability: [src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/XSSAPI.java:30-231], [src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/XSSFilter.java:21-73].
- Filtering implementation sanitizes HTML using AntiSamy’s scan/cleaning functions (HTML parsing/sanitization, not code execution): [src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/HtmlToHtmlContentContext.java:34-83], [src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/PolicyHandler.java:28-56], [src/main/java/org/apache/sling/xss/impl/XSSFilterImpl.java:92-201].
- Build/dependency configuration explicitly excludes BeanShell (bsh) from imports and from key dependencies (reducing risk of embedded scripting/code-eval surfaces): [pom.xml:83-99], [pom.xml:128-215].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repo contains a production HTTP endpoint (/v1/cs/configs) that uses attacker-supplied request parameters (tenant/group/dataId/tag) as filesystem path segments for on-disk config caching and direct file streaming. Validation explicitly allows '.' characters, so values like ".." pass, enabling traversal outside the intended cache directory and reaching filesystem read/write sinks without robust canonical-path containment.
EVIDENCE:
- Production entry point and attacker-controlled parameters: ConfigController exposes GET /v1/cs/configs with request parameters dataId, group, tenant, tag, and passes them onward after ParamUtils validation: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigController.java:194-211]. The base path resolves to /v1/cs/configs: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/constant/Constants.java:112-121].
- Validation allows '..' segments: ParamUtils allows letters/digits plus validChars {'_', '-', '.', ':'}; since '.' is allowed, the string ".." is considered valid. No check rejects ".." specifically: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/ParamUtils.java:31-65]. Tenant/tag checks reuse the same isValid() logic: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/ParamUtils.java:97-106] and [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/ParamUtils.java:159-168].
- Path construction from untrusted segments (no containment/canonicalization): DiskUtil builds cache file paths by chaining new File(base, segment) for tenant/group/dataId/tag directly from inputs: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/DiskUtil.java:139-151].
- Filesystem read sink reachable from HTTP: When PropertyUtil.isDirectRead() is false, ConfigServletInner selects a DiskUtil target*File and opens it with FileInputStream, streaming it to the HTTP response: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigServletInner.java:214-219] and [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigServletInner.java:245-257].
- The file-based branch is intended for non-standalone or non-embedded-storage deployments: isDirectRead() is only true for standalone && embeddedStorage, otherwise the file path is used: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/PropertyUtil.java:241-247].
- Escape example (demonstrating CWE-22 “escape” condition): With tenant="..", group="..", dataId="etc", tag="passwd" (all pass ParamUtils.isValid), DiskUtil.targetTagFile constructs a path that resolves via '..' to /etc/passwd, escaping the intended cache directory, and ConfigServletInner will attempt to read it when isDirectRead()==false. (Escape is enabled by the direct use of ".." segments in DiskUtil path concatenation: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/DiskUtil.java:139-151]).
- Filesystem write sink also present via on-disk dump/cache: DiskUtil.saveTagToDisk writes attacker-controlled content to the computed targetTagFile: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/DiskUtil.java:73-77]. ConfigCacheService.dumpTag invokes saveTagToDisk when not direct-read: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/service/ConfigCacheService.java:191-212]. DumpConfigHandler calls dumpTag for tagged config events: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/service/dump/DumpConfigHandler.java:70-106].

(Additional artifact-scope issue, independent of the HTTP endpoint above): The shipped jar module `nacos-sys` contains a public unzip API (DiskUtils.decompress) that writes ZipEntry names to disk under outputDir without Zip Slip defenses: [/sys/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/sys/utils/DiskUtils.java:421-437] and the module is packaged as a jar artifact: [/sys/pom.xml:29-33].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Repository code does not expose any production-reachable path where attacker-controlled input influences OS command/process execution. Direct Java process-execution APIs (Runtime.exec / ProcessBuilder) are not present in the Java sources, and YAML parsing components use SnakeYAML SafeConstructor with explicit rejection of custom tags, preventing gadget-based execution. The only OS process execution observed is in operator-invoked distribution startup scripts.
EVIDENCE: 
- Operator-run startup per docs: README shows starting Nacos via local shell command `sh startup.sh -m standalone` (administrator/operator action), not a remote interface [/workdir/repo/README.md:36-68].
- Startup script executes the Java process via `nohup` and builds JVM args from CLI flags; this is a local admin script (trusted input per test threat model) [/workdir/repo/distribution/bin/startup.sh:54-146].
- Repo-wide Java source search for common process-execution sinks found no matches (empty result) [/evidence/artifacts/cwe78_search_summary.txt:1-10].
- Client YAML parsing uses SnakeYAML SafeConstructor (blocks arbitrary type construction) and throws on invalid constructor tags [/workdir/repo/client/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/client/config/impl/YmlChangeParser.java:48-76].
- Server YAML parsing utility extends SafeConstructor and only registers a specific tag (ConfigMetadata), rejecting unexpected tags; construction logic only reads scalar values into POJOs (no process execution) [/workdir/repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/YamlParserUtil.java:45-78], [/workdir/repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/YamlParserUtil.java:93-134].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repo includes a production HTTP endpoint (/v1/cs/configs) that can return attacker-supplied configuration content as Content-Type text/html without any sanitization/escaping. Because attackers can publish configs with type=html and arbitrary content, a victim who retrieves/views that config in a browser will execute attacker-controlled script in the Nacos origin (stored XSS / CWE-79).
EVIDENCE:
- The configuration API is served under /v1/cs/configs: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/constant/Constants.java:112-121].
- The server explicitly supports an HTML config type: ConfigType includes HTML("html"): [/api/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/api/config/ConfigType.java:29-59].
- The publish endpoint accepts attacker-controlled "content" and "type" parameters and keeps a valid type (including html) instead of rejecting it: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigController.java:119-166].
- HTML types are mapped to the HTTP content type text/html;charset=UTF-8: [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/enums/FileTypeEnum.java:60-70] and [/common/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/common/http/param/MediaType.java:39-47].
- When serving configs, the implementation sets the response Content-Type based on the stored config type and writes the raw config content to the HTTP response body (no escaping/sanitization): [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigServletInner.java:146-152] and [/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigServletInner.java:249-257].
- The project includes an auth system with separate users/roles (supporting the attacker/victim model of different authenticated users), e.g., the user-management controller: [/plugin-default-impl/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/plugin/auth/impl/controller/UserController.java:67-110].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Repo is a Java Mustache templating library; no production entry points take attacker-controlled path/entry names and reach OS filesystem I/O. The only runtime filesystem I/O found is in an optional JMustache hot-reload extension intended for development; it builds paths from template metadata/partial names originating from developer-controlled templates, not from any repo-documented remote/untrusted interface.
EVIDENCE: 
- JStachio’s public API renders from a model object and does not accept arbitrary filesystem paths (library, not a server): [/api/jstachio/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstachio/JStachio.java:16-48].
- Optional runtime extension for hot-reloading templates explicitly warns to disable in production: [/opt/jstachio-jmustache/src/main/java/io/jstach/opt/jmustache/JMustacheRenderer.java:21-52].
- In that extension, partial names (from template content) are used as a path component with no traversal neutralization (candidate sink), but this requires attacker control of template/partial names: [/opt/jstachio-jmustache/src/main/java/io/jstach/opt/jmustache/CompilerAdapter.java:61-87].
- The extension performs filesystem reads using Path.of(sourcePath, templatePath) and Files.newInputStream(path) without containment checks (candidate sink), but the templatePath comes from TemplateInfo/template files rather than any repo-documented untrusted input channel: [/opt/jstachio-jmustache/src/main/java/io/jstach/opt/jmustache/Loader.java:53-85].
- TemplateInfo describes templatePath as resolved by the annotation processor (developer/build-time controlled) and its normalizePath only strips a leading slash (no suggestion of untrusted runtime paths): [/api/jstachio/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstachio/TemplateInfo.java:28-52].

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repo ships a Mustache templating engine whose default “HTML escaping” contract is used for rendering text/html, but the provided HTML escaper does not escape apostrophes ('). This allows attacker-controlled data to break out of common HTML contexts (e.g., single-quoted attributes) and introduce executable script/event-handler content, i.e., CWE-79.
EVIDENCE:
- The project explicitly claims “out of the box escaping for HTML … per the mustache spec” via `io.jstach.jstachio.escapers.Html` when using the runtime (the normal/default mode). [/workdir/repo/api/annotation/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstache/JStache.java:386-397]
- If content type is unspecified, a “spec based HTML content type will be used” (so HTML escaping is the default behavior in typical usage). [/workdir/repo/api/annotation/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstache/JStacheConfig.java:127-137]
- The runtime Escaper API documents that the default escaper is `Html#of()` and that the escaper is not given template context (so it is used regardless of whether a variable is placed in element text vs attribute contexts). [/workdir/repo/api/jstachio/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstachio/Escaper.java:16-38]
- The shipped public HTML content type/escaper (`Html`) states it “simply escapes” only `"`, `>`, `<`, and `&` (no apostrophe), despite being used for `text/html`. [/workdir/repo/api/jstachio/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstachio/escapers/Html.java:9-35]
- The actual escaping implementation only handles `&`, `<`, `>`, and `"` and leaves `'` unchanged. [/workdir/repo/api/jstachio/src/main/java/io/jstach/jstachio/escapers/HtmlEscaper.java:10-78]

Why this is CWE-79 exploitable (artifact scope): Because the library is intended to render HTML templates with untrusted model data, failing to escape `'` makes escaped variables unsafe in standard HTML contexts such as single-quoted attributes (e.g., `<div data-x='{{value}}'>`), where an attacker-supplied value containing `' onmouseover='alert(1)` becomes executable JavaScript in a victim’s browser.

summary='**Evaluating HTML escaping vulnerabilities**\n\nIn jstachio mode, `contentTypeProvideCall` offers an escaper for HTML types like Html.of(). Default `text/html` templates rely on HtmlEscaper that doesn’t escape the single quote (\'), which raises a potential XSS risk if inserted into single-quoted attributes. While it\'s likely that template authors can allow single quotes, the issue remains. I need to ensure `Html` is the default type, as recommended. However, there\'s ambiguity with unquoted attributes too, so the risk remains plausible.\n\n**Analyzing mustache\'s escaping behavior**\n\nI’m looking into whether mustache is truly content agnostic and doesn\'t differentiate in how it handles attributes, which suggests it might not be safe for those contexts. The spec mentions flexible escaping rules, focusing on whitespace rather than preventing quote injection. Even if untrusted strings could cause XSS in certain contexts, mustache escapes characters like < and >. However, if a script tag includes `</script>`, it may still create vulnerabilities. So, I think some caution is definitely warranted.\n\n**Examining JS string injection risks**\n\nI\'m considering how single quotes and double quotes work with JavaScript strings inside `<script>` tags. It seems that HTML escape only converts double quotes but leaves single quotes vulnerable. If an attacker finds a way to insert a string like `\';alert(1);//`, they could close the JS string and run malicious code. The HTML escape doesn\'t actually preserve the needed protections. Additionally, even if entities are used, they aren\'t decoded within script tags. This really raises concerns about exploitation if variables are inserted into single-quoted strings.\n\n**Clarifying script data and character references**\n\nI’m pondering whether HTML character references are parsed in script data. It seems like in script elements, the parser does recognize character references, but according to the spec, they actually don’t get parsed. So in a script like `<script>var x = "<"</script>`, JavaScript sees `<` as is, not as `<`. This means that escaping quotes with HTML entities like `'` would protect against string breaks, since the actual apostrophe character would still be needed for exploitation.\n\n**Assessing escaping and injection risks**\n\nIf I escape an apostrophe to `'`, it wouldn’t close a JavaScript string since JavaScript sees `&`. This might help prevent some injection attacks, but HTML escaping isn\'t always suitable for script contexts because it doesn\'t escape backslashes. Many template engines have context-aware escaping, but mustache lacks this, leaving it vulnerable to XSS in JavaScript. While typical usage may risk misuse, the promise of safe HTML output remains. I need to gather evidence that highlights missing escapes in attributes or JavaScript strings, particularly focusing on plausible scenarios of untrusted input leading to exploitation, especially in single-quoted contexts.', signature='rs_0e1f26816273d5c9016955a1d0e6f08192a34ba70d7da410fd', redacted=True)]...

metadata.test_description:
There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).
